summary: Sirach 36 begins as a communal prayer asking the Lord, “the God of all,” to show mercy to Israel, confront hostile nations, gather Jacob’s tribes, and restore Jerusalem and Zion. The chapter then turns to wisdom comparisons about discernment, false speech, marriage, household stability, and the vulnerability of a person with “no nest.”
whyItMatters: This chapter shows how Sirach can move from public prayer for Israel to ordinary-life instruction without treating them as separate worlds. It also exposes a difficult feature of the book: some counsel about women and marriage comes from an ancient male household setting and should be read with that distance in view.

context.author: Yeshua (Jesus) son of Eleazar son of Sira, a Jerusalem teacher and scribe; the book was later translated into Greek by his unnamed grandson.
context.audience: Students seeking disciplined wisdom in Jerusalem, and Greek-reading Jews in Egypt or the wider diaspora through the grandson’s translation.
context.date: The Hebrew work was composed in the early second century BC and was likely complete around 180–175 BC. The grandson arrived in Egypt around 132 BC and translated it during his stay.
context.setting: Jerusalem and the wider Jewish world under Hellenistic rule, with temple worship, Torah study, and Greek-speaking Mediterranean culture in view.
context.literaryForm: Wisdom instruction that includes prayer, poetic teaching, maxims, vivid comparisons, and practical social counsel.

outline.heading: Prayer for the nations to know God
outline.note: The speaker asks for mercy, for the nations to see God’s power, and for new signs and wonders.

outline.heading: Judgment on enemies
outline.note: The prayer asks God to act against adversaries, enemies, and proud rulers who deny any authority beyond themselves.

outline.heading: Restoration of Jacob, Jerusalem, and Zion
outline.note: The speaker asks God to gather Israel, show compassion to Jerusalem, fulfill prophetic words, and answer the prayer of God’s servants.

outline.heading: Discernment and false speech
outline.note: Food-tasting becomes a comparison for how an understanding heart recognizes false speech, while a contrary heart brings heaviness.

outline.heading: Wife, household, and stability
outline.note: The chapter closes with counsel about choosing a wife, the value of kindness and humility, household support, and the insecurity of a man who has no settled home.

keyVerses.text: Let them know you, as we also have known you, that there is no God but only you, O God.
keyVerses.why: This line states the goal of the opening prayer: that the nations would recognize the one God known by Israel.

keyVerses.text: Gather all the tribes of Jacob together, and take them for your inheritance, as from the beginning.
keyVerses.why: The prayer turns from judgment on enemies to the restoration and gathering of Israel.

keyVerses.text: Listen, O Lord, to the prayer of your servants, according to the blessing of Aaron concerning your people; and all those who are on the earth will know that you are the Lord, the eternal God.
keyVerses.why: This verse gathers the prayer’s concerns: God’s hearing, Israel’s blessing, and worldwide recognition of the Lord.

keyVerses.text: The mouth tastes meats taken in hunting, so does an understanding heart detect false speech.
keyVerses.why: This proverb marks the shift from national prayer to practical wisdom about discernment.

questions.question: Why does the chapter begin with a prayer instead of a proverb?
questions.answer: Sirach includes more than short maxims; it also contains prayers, hymns, and longer reflections. Here the speaker asks the Lord for mercy, for the nations to know God, and for Israel and Jerusalem to be restored before the chapter turns to ordinary-life wisdom.

questions.question: Who is being addressed as “the God of all”?
questions.answer: The prayer addresses the Lord as God over all peoples, not only over Israel. That is why the nations appear throughout the opening section: they are asked to fear, see, know, and finally recognize the Lord as “the eternal God.”

questions.question: What does “your fear” mean here?
questions.answer: In this prayer the nations are asked to recognize the Lord’s power and authority. Verse 3 asks God to lift his hand against them, while verse 5 asks them to know that there is no other God. In that setting, fear includes alarm before divine power as well as recognition of God’s rule.

questions.question: Why does the prayer ask for wrath, destruction, and crushed rulers?
questions.answer: The prayer speaks from the side of a harmed people asking God to act against adversaries and enemies. It names those who “harm your people” and rulers who say, “There is no one but ourselves.” Its requests for consuming fire and crushed rulers are severe. They belong to an appeal for God’s intervention, not a command for students to carry out the destruction.

questions.question: What is meant by “Gather all the tribes of Jacob together”?
questions.answer: The line asks God to reunite Jacob’s tribes and take them as God’s inheritance “as from the beginning.” In the chapter’s movement, this request follows the plea for judgment on enemies and leads into compassion for Israel, Jerusalem, and Zion.

questions.question: Why are Jerusalem and Zion important in this prayer?
questions.answer: The chapter calls Jerusalem “the city of your sanctuary” and “the place of your rest.” Zion is linked with God’s oracles, God’s people, and God’s glory, so the prayer treats the city as central to Israel’s worship and public hope.

questions.question: How does verse 19 describe wisdom?
questions.answer: It compares discernment to tasting food. Just as the mouth can distinguish meats, “an understanding heart” can detect false speech; wisdom here is practical perception, especially in speech and trust.

questions.question: How should readers handle the sayings about women and wives?
questions.answer: The chapter praises a wife whose speech has kindness and humility and calls a wife a treasure and support. It also ranks daughters from a prospective husband’s point of view. These lines reflect an ancient male household perspective: they value women in relation to a man’s marriage and household, rather than offering a full account of women’s lives or agency.

questions.question: What is the point of the final image about having “no nest”?
questions.answer: The last verse compares an unsettled man to a robber who moves from city to city and cannot be trusted. Within the chapter’s closing section, the image contrasts household stability with wandering insecurity.

glossary.def: The peoples outside Israel named in the opening prayer; the speaker asks God to act so they see divine power.
Israel described through Jacob’s tribes; the prayer asks that they be gathered together and received as God’s inheritance.
A holy place connected here with Jerusalem, called “the city of your sanctuary.”
Authoritative words associated here with Zion and God’s people.
Speech that an understanding heart is able to detect, compared to the mouth tasting food.
An image for settled belonging or home in the final proverb about a man who lodges wherever night finds him.
